nodes.bodyText:
Summary
The nightly ROCm manywheel-py3_15-rocm7_1-build / manywheel-py3_15t-rocm7_1-build binary builds fail while installing build requirements, when numpy is built from source. numpy's meson build runs a Cython sanity check that resolves its python3 dependency via pkg-config, and the ROCm manylinux image (pytorch/manylinux2_28-builder:rocm7.1) carries the distro's system python3-devel (Python 3.6) on pkg-config's default search path, so the check picks up 3.6 and fails:
Determining dependency 'python3' with pkg-config
`pkg-config --cflags python3` -> -I/usr/include/python3.6m
Run-time dependency python3 found: YES 3.6
sanity_check_for_cython.c:23:6: error: #error Cython requires Python 3.8+.
../meson.build:1:0: ERROR: Compiler cython cannot compile programs.

This happens in .ci/manywheel/build_install_deps.py (the pip install -qU -r requirements-build.txt step), which is the entry point .ci/manywheel/build.sh uses for the ROCm/CUDA/CPU/XPU manywheel builds.
Root cause

cp315 (Python 3.15) has no numpy wheel on any index (numpy 2.5.0 and 2.5.1 are sdist-only), so any fresh numpy install is built from source.
requirements-build.txt lists numpy unpinned, installed with pip install -U, so it resolves to the newest release.
The failure is not a code change and not an image change — it was triggered by an upstream numpy 2.5.1 release (2026-07-04 17:06 UTC). Before that, pip install -U numpy kept the image's prebuilt numpy 2.5.0 (a no-op). After 2.5.1 published, -U upgraded to 2.5.1 and built it from source, hitting the ROCm image's system-python3.6 pkg-config collision.

Passing vs failing builds (same image digest)
Both pulled the identical image pytorch/manylinux2_28-builder:rocm7.1 (sha256:33d484927bb614089caca3d33e705a1aea12e15d27278844955e034878f682b8):




Run
When
numpy
Result




Green
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/28700338171
2026-07-04 08:20 UTC (before 2.5.1)
reused prebuilt 2.5.0, no source build
✅


Red
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/28734817308
2026-07-05 08:30 UTC (after 2.5.1)
-U upgraded to 2.5.1 → built from source
❌



Fix
PR #189722 pins cp315 numpy to the image's prebuilt 2.5.0 on ROCm (DESIRED_CUDA=*rocm*) in .ci/manywheel/build_install_deps.py, so the -U upgrade can't pull the wheel-less newer release and no source build happens. Other architectures and Python versions are unchanged.
A more durable, arch-agnostic alternative would be to make the from-source build resolve pkg-config python3 to the interpreter being built (prepend the target interpreter's pkgconfig dir), or to remove/relocate the stray system python3.pc in the ROCm manylinux base image (rocm/dev-almalinux-8:*-complete).
Environment

Image: pytorch/manylinux2_28-builder:rocm7.1
Python: cp315 / cp315t (3.15)
numpy: 2.5.1 (sdist, no cp315 wheel)
Jobs: manywheel-py3_15-rocm7_1-build, manywheel-py3_15t-rocm7_1-build

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
On Apple Silicon MPS, torch.nn.functional.linear applied to a 3D input of decode shape [B, 1, K] is up to ~8.5x slower than the mathematically identical 2D op [B, K], and than torch.matmul(x, w.t()) on the same 3D tensor. The cost ramps ~linearly with B and then snaps back to GEMM once B crosses a threshold (~16). It directly throttles on-device LLM token generation
It is specific to

MPS
F.linear (which on MPS routes to _mps_linear)
half precision (fp32 is unaffected)
3D half input with small non-batch dims (M == 1 is the worst/most-persistent case)

Environment
PyTorch : 2.14.0a0 (source build; also present on 2.10.x)
OS      : macOS 26.4 (25E246)
Device  : Apple M4 Pro (MPS)
dtype   : bfloat16 (fp16 identical; fp32 unaffected)

Minimal reproduction
import time, torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
dev, dt = "mps", torch.bfloat16
K, N = 5120, 17408                              # Qwen3-14B gate: [.,K] @ [K,N]
W = torch.randn(N, K, device=dev, dtype=dt)     # nn.Linear weight [out, in]

def timed(fn, warmup=10, iters=30):
    for _ in range(warmup): fn()
    torch.mps.synchronize(); ts=[]
    for _ in range(iters):
        torch.mps.synchronize(); t=time.perf_counter()
        fn(); torch.mps.synchronize(); ts.append((time.perf_counter()-t)*1e3)
    return sorted(ts)[len(ts)//2]

print(f"{'B':>4} {'F.linear_3d':>12} {'F.linear_2d':>12} {'matmul_3d':>10} {'3d/2d':>6}")
for B in (1,4,8,14,16,32,64):
    x3 = torch.randn(B,1,K,device=dev,dtype=dt)  # [B,1,K] decode shape
    x2 = x3.squeeze(1)                            # [B,K] (zero-copy view)
    l3 = timed(lambda: F.linear(x3, W))
    l2 = timed(lambda: F.linear(x2, W))
    m3 = timed(lambda: torch.matmul(x3, W.t()))
    print(f"{B:>4} {l3:>12.2f} {l2:>12.2f} {m3:>10.2f} {l3/l2:>5.1f}x")
Output (M4 Pro, macOS 26.4, bf16):
   B  F.linear_3d  F.linear_2d   matmul_3d  3d/2d
   1         0.89         0.91        0.93   1.0x
   4         3.00         0.97        0.97   3.1x
   8         5.76         0.94        0.93   6.1x
  14         9.91         1.17        1.18   8.5x
  16         1.15         1.14        1.15   1.0x
  32         1.28         1.29        1.30   1.0x
  64         1.97         1.95        1.96   1.0x


Expected: F.linear([B,1,K]) costs ~the same as F.linear([B,K]) and
matmul([B,1,K], w.t()) — a [B,1]×N output is a trivial reshape from a
[B]×N GEMM.
Actual: F.linear([B,1,K]) ramps ~linearly in B (each batch element run
as an independent GEMV) and only snaps to GEMM performance past a width-
dependent B threshold. matmul and 2D F.linear stay flat.

Analysis


F.linear only. torch.matmul, torch.mm, torch.addmm on the same logical op do not show the linear-per-batch ramp.
3D half input with small non-batch dims. M == 1 ([B,1,K]) is the worst and most persistent case, but [B,2,K] also ramps at low B and snaps earlier (~B=5); [B,8,K] tracks the efficient GEMM sooner. A leading singleton [1,B,K] (middle dim = B) is flat. The pathology is the small-leading-dims 3D layout staying below the N-dependent GEMM threshold; seq=1 decode (M==1) sits in it for the widest B range.
Half precision only. At B=8 gate: bf16 = 6.1x, fp16 = 6.0x, fp32 = 1.0x (no cliff).
Threshold scales with output width N. Snap-back B is None only for  N = 512; ~16 for N ∈ [1024, 17408]; ~10 for N ≥ 32768. So the per-layer snap differs by width (MLP N=17408 ~16, lm_head N=151936 ~10), and a full decode step's summed
cost peaks around batch 8–14 before the widest ops flip to GEMM.

Source localization
aten::linear on MPS maps to _mps_linear (native_functions.yaml → aten/src/ATen/native/mps/operations/Linear.mm)
For the decode case (macOS 15+, contiguous, non-complex, half) _mps_linear takes the nograph fast path _mps_linear_nograph, which hands the raw 3D [B,1,K] NDArray to MPSNDArrayMatrixMultiplication (weight transposed, broadcast over the leading batch dim) → per-batch GEMV.
A flatten-to-2D perf workaround for exactly this 3D case already exists, but only in the graph branch of _mps_linear (reached on macOS < 15):
// graph branch -- the perf workaround exists here:
bool doReshape = input.dim() > 4;
if (!doReshape && is_bias_defined) {
  // workaround to improve the performance with 3D+ inputs
  doReshape = input_size.size() > 2 && input_size[0] > 1 &&
              input_size[1] >= 1 && input_size[1] <= 32 && bias.dim() <= 1;
}
The nograph fast path has no equivalent perf flatten. Its only flatten, needs_nd_workaround(input), is a non-determinism fix gated to the Apple10 (M5+) GPU family (#180776) — it does not fire on M4 and is unrelated to this GEMV perf issue. So on M4 / macOS 26 a contiguous half [B,1,K] reaches _mps_linear_nograph with no flatten → the per-batch GEMV cliff.
Proposed fix
The nograph fast path already has a flatten-to-2D branch, it is just gated to the M5+ non-determinism case (needs_nd_workaround). Broadening that gate to any >2D input fixes the GEMV cliff and subsumes the existing workaround. One-line change in _mps_linear:
-    if (needs_nd_workaround(input) && (!kernel_bias.defined() || kernel_bias.dim() <= 1)) {
+    if (input.dim() > 2 && (!kernel_bias.defined() || kernel_bias.dim() <= 1)) {
       auto input2d = input.flatten(0, -2);    // [B,1,K] -> [B,K]  (zero-copy view)
       auto output2d = output.flatten(0, -2);  // [B,1,N] -> [B,N]
       _mps_linear_nograph(input2d, weight, kernel_bias, output2d);
     } else {
       _mps_linear_nograph(input, weight, kernel_bias, output);
     }
flatten(0, -2) on a contiguous input is a zero-copy view.
Verification
(a) Related PR #184631 (drop strides() in _mps_linear_nograph) does not fix this. A canonically-strided [B,1,K] never takes the strided NDArray path that PR targets, so the cliff is unchanged: F.linear_3d still 6.2x at B=8, 8.5x at B=14, snapping at 16. (That PR fixes a different problem — non-canonically strided contiguous inputs, e.g. a B=1 transpose in MultiheadAttention, #181725.)
(b) The flatten fix above eliminates it. With the gate broadened, F.linear on [B,1,K] matches 2D and torch.matmul at every batch, with no large-batch regression (M4 Pro, bf16, ms):
   B | F.linear_3d | F.linear_2d | matmul_3d | 3d/2d
   1 |        0.94 |        0.94 |      0.97 | 1.0x
   8 |        0.93 |        0.93 |      0.92 | 1.0x    (was 5.8 ms / 6.2x)
  14 |        1.16 |        1.16 |      1.18 | 1.0x    (was 9.9 ms / 8.5x)
  16 |        1.17 |        1.17 |      1.18 | 1.0x
  32 |        1.29 |        1.29 |      1.31 | 1.0x
  64 |        1.97 |        1.96 |      1.97 | 1.0x

Output is bit-identical (torch.allclose / torch.equal), since the flatten is a pure reshape.
Related Issues

#186541 (open, "Port all MPSGraph matmuls to Metal") — benchmark table shows MPSGraph matmul slow on GEMV (M==1) / small-batch bmm.
#184631 (open, "Skip strided NDArray path in _mps_linear_nograph when inputs are contiguous") — same function, but a different cause (non-canonical
strides). Tested: does not fix this GEMV cliff (see Verification).
#181725 (open) — nn.MultiheadAttention ~9x slower at B=1; the case #184631 fixes (B=1 strided F.linear), distinct from this M=1 GEMV cliff.
#188728 (open) — F.linear ignores PYTORCH_MPS_PREFER_METAL.
#117837 (merged) — origin of the graph-branch input_size[1] <= 32 flatten workaround. #180776 (closed) / #181466 (merged) — the M5+ >2D half linear non-determinism flatten this fix generalizes.

🐛 Describe the bug
Look, I'm gonna be straight with y'all. Done spent 12+ hours yesterday getting Intel Arc Pro B70 working on Ubuntu. Got the GPU detected. Got it initialized. Got PyTorch XPU loaded and running. Then the moment I tried to actually use it, boom:
RuntimeError: The device (Intel(R) Graphics [0x7d67]) doesn't support querying the available free memory.
This ain't right. Y'all advertise Arc XPU support like it's ready to go, but torch.xpu.memory_allocated() doesn't exist. Not stubbed out. Not half-working. Flat-out doesn't exist at the C++ level. And when Transformers tries to load a model, it calls this function on startup. Game over.
I tried every workaround I could think of:
Monkey-patching before imports? Nope, still hits C++ code that ain't there.
Wrapping with contextlib.suppress? Still crashes — the C++ layer's throwing an exception.
Different IPEX versions? Same problem.
Verified the GPU works? Yeah. sycl-ls sees it. device_count() works. Everything works until you try to query memory.
Here's the bottom line: Arc XPU can't do ML workloads on Linux right now. Not with Transformers. Not with any major library that queries GPU memory. The feature is broken.
Either implement the memory management APIs at the C++ level and make this work, or stop claiming Arc support is functional. Don't advertise features that don't work and waste developers' time chasing ghosts.
System: Intel Arc Pro B70, Ubuntu 24.04, PyTorch 2.8.0+xpu, IPEX 2.8.10+xpu
Fix it or don't claim it works.
Upset Texan.

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
torch.compile with the inductor backend produces a numerical discrepancy in F.gelu(x) for input values near x ≈ -5.53. In eager mode, F.gelu(-5.53) produces -0.0 (negative zero, 0x80000000). In inductor, it produces a tiny negative value (≈ -1.65e-7). When followed by torch.sign(), this causes sign(-0.0) = 0 in eager vs sign(tiny_negative) = -1 in inductor — a difference of 1.0 in the output.
In the original fuzzer-generated model, the chain log2(x) → log2(result) → div → gelu → sign → sigmoid produces max_diff=0.23 at output index 13 (shape [23, 64, 62]).
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

# Values from the original computation chain where gelu produces -0.0
x = torch.tensor([-5.533906936645508, -5.531643390655518], dtype=torch.float32)

class BugModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        return torch.sign(F.gelu(x))

model = BugModel()

with torch.no_grad():
    ref = model(x)  # eager

with torch.no_grad():
    aot_out = torch.compile(model, backend="aot_eager")(x)

with torch.no_grad():
    ind_out = torch.compile(model, mode="default")(x)

print(f"Input:  {x.tolist()}")
print(f"Eager:  {ref.tolist()}   (gelu produces -0.0, sign(-0.0)=0)")
print(f"aot:    {aot_out.tolist()}")
print(f"Induct: {ind_out.tolist()}   (gelu produces ~-1.65e-7, sign(tiny_neg)=-1)")
print(f"aot vs ref: same={torch._dynamo.utils.same(ref.double(), aot_out.double())}")
print(f"ind  vs ref: same={torch._dynamo.utils.same(ref.double(), ind_out.double())}")
print(f"max_diff (ind vs ref): {(ref.double() - ind_out.double()).abs().max().item():.6f}")

# Also the full chain from the original source
print("\n=== Full chain from original source ===")
torch.manual_seed(42)
v6 = torch.randn(23, 64, 62, dtype=torch.float32, device="cpu")

class FullChainModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        a = torch.log2(x)
        b = torch.log2(a)
        c = torch.div(a, b)
        d = F.gelu(c)
        e = torch.sign(d)
        return torch.sigmoid(e)

full_model = FullChainModel()
with torch.no_grad():
    full_ref = full_model(v6)
full_ind = torch.compile(full_model, mode="default")
with torch.no_grad():
    full_ind_out = full_ind(v6)

print(f"Full chain ind vs ref: same={torch._dynamo.utils.same(full_ref.double(), full_ind_out.double())}")
print(f"max_diff: {(full_ref.double() - full_ind_out.double()).abs().max().item():.6f}")

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
torch.compile with the inductor backend produces large numerical discrepancies (up to ~108 in absolute value) for the expression torch.reciprocal(elu(x, alpha) + exp(elu(x, alpha))) compared to both eager and aot_eager backends.
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class BugModule(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, alpha: float = 1.24):
        super().__init__()
        self.alpha = alpha

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        elu_val = F.elu(x, alpha=self.alpha)
        exp_elu = torch.exp(elu_val)
        v = torch.add(elu_val, exp_elu)
        return torch.reciprocal(v)

torch.manual_seed(42)
x = torch.randn(24, 57, 37, dtype=torch.float32, device="cpu")

model = BugModule(alpha=1.24)

with torch.no_grad():
    eager_out = model(x)

with torch.no_grad():
    aot_out = torch.compile(model, backend="aot_eager")(x)

with torch.no_grad():
    ind_out = torch.compile(model, mode="default")(x)

# fp64 reference
x_fp64 = x.to(torch.float64)
model_fp64 = BugModule(alpha=1.24)
with torch.no_grad():
    fp64_ref = model_fp64(x_fp64).to(torch.float32)

print(f"max |aot_eager - inductor|  : {(aot_out - ind_out).abs().max().item():.4f}")
print(f"max |eager     - aot_eager| : {(eager_out - aot_out).abs().max().item():.6f}")
print(f"max |fp64_ref  - inductor|  : {(fp64_ref - ind_out).abs().max().item():.4f}")

The downstream projects (tritonbench, fbtriton, etc) uses PyTorch Nightly RoCM 7.2 in the CI.
We found that our CI couldn't properly download the nightly wheel using uv pip June-July, the latest usable wheel is 20260513.
The command line (using Python 3.12):
uv pip install --pre --no-cache-dir torch -i https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/rocm7.2

🐛 Describe the bug
When torch.nn.RMSNorm is applied to a bfloat16 tensor with a small variance (e.g., standard deviation around 0.05), the output diverges significantly (by ~1.7x) from both the mathematical definition of RMSNorm and PyTorch's own float32 output.
This appears to be caused by a severe precision loss or underflow during the internal sum-of-squares accumulation when the input is natively in bfloat16.
Minimal Reproducible Example
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(42) # seed to get the same results as me (although results are consistant across a variety of seeds)

# Params
D = 32
B, H, N = 2, 4, 1

# Downcast a tensor with a very small variance in float32 to bfloat16
x_fp32 = torch.randn(B, H, N, D, dtype=torch.float32) * 0.058
x_bf16 = x_fp32.to(torch.bfloat16)
norm_layer = nn.RMSNorm(D, elementwise_affine=False)
# Native RMSNorm acting on bfloat16 directly (buggy)
out_pytorch_bf16 = norm_layer(x_bf16)
# Native RMSNorm acting on float32 (stable)
out_pytorch_fp32 = norm_layer(x_fp32)
# Manual RMSNorm implementation in float32
var_manual = (x_fp32 ** 2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
out_manual_fp32 = x_fp32 / torch.sqrt(var_manual + 1e-5)
print("PyTorch bfloat16 output [0,0,0,:4]:")
print(out_pytorch_bf16[0,0,0,:4].float().tolist())
print("\nPyTorch float32 output [0,0,0,:4]:")
print(out_pytorch_fp32[0,0,0,:4].tolist())
print("\nManual float32 output [0,0,0,:4]:")
print(out_manual_fp32[0,0,0,:4].tolist())
ratio = out_manual_fp32[0,0,0,:4] / out_pytorch_bf16[0,0,0,:4].float()
print(f"\nDiscrepancy Ratio (Manual fp32 / PyTorch bf16): {ratio.mean().item():.3f}x")
Output
PyTorch bfloat16 output [0,0,0,:4]:
[1.03125, 0.796875, 0.48046875, -1.125]
PyTorch float32 output [0,0,0,:4]:
[1.771738052368164, 1.3675109148025513, 0.8281811475753784, -1.9359601736068726]
Manual float32 output [0,0,0,:4]:
[1.7695422172546387, 1.3658159971237183, 0.8271547555923462, -1.933560848236084]
Discrepancy Ratio (Manual fp32 / PyTorch bf16): 1.718x

Versions
I used PyTorch: 2.6.0+cu124, on a RTX 4060 gpu.
Hopefully this will get resolved soon. Although the standard way is to use fp32 for RMSNorm regardless, it's still a bug (Took me a bunch of time to debug why my custom inference kernal mismatched naive pytorch by more than quantization noise😵‍💫).

🐛 Describe the bug
A dtype-converting copy from MPS to CPU can silently overwrite the source MPS
tensor when the CPU destination has a nonzero buffer offset and its element size
is less than or equal to the source element size. copy_ should never modify its
source.
The CPU destination is correct in this example, which makes the source corruption
easy to miss:
import torch

expected = torch.arange(8, dtype=torch.float32) + 0.25
source = expected.to("mps")

# Four-byte aligned but nonzero destination byte offset. This makes the trigger
# deterministic instead of depending on where a fresh CPU tensor is allocated.
destination_storage = torch.empty(10, dtype=torch.float16)
destination = destination_storage[2:]

destination.copy_(source)
torch.mps.synchronize()

print("destination:", destination.tolist())
print("source before:", expected.tolist())
print("source after: ", source.cpu().tolist())
print("source unchanged:", torch.equal(source.cpu(), expected))
Output on the current nightly:
destination: [0.25, 1.25, 2.25, 3.25, 4.25, 5.25, 6.25, 7.25]
source before: [0.25, 1.25, 2.25, 3.25, 4.25, 5.25, 6.25, 7.25]
source after:  [0.031299591064453125, 64.1259765625, 3076.265625, 49222.25, 4.25, 5.25, 6.25, 7.25]
source unchanged: False

Expected behavior: destination contains the fp16 conversion and source remains
bit-for-bit equal to expected.
The same source mutation also reproduces for the equal-width float32-to-int32
conversion.
This also affects ordinary .to(device="cpu", dtype=...) calls when the allocated
CPU destination has a nonzero wrapped-buffer offset. Consequently, making a
dtype-converted host copy for export, checkpoint processing, or inspection can
silently change live MPS model state and affect later computation.
Source diagnosis
In
copy_from_mps_,
maybeCastedSourceBuffer initially aliases sourceBuffer. When a direct cast into
the wrapped CPU destination is unavailable, a temporary is allocated only for a
widening conversion (src.element_size() < dst.element_size()). Narrowing and
equal-width dtype conversions therefore run exec_unary_kernel_raw with the live
source buffer as both the input storage and cast destination, overwriting the
source bytes.
The cast should use destination storage directly when that is valid; otherwise it
needs a destination-typed temporary MPS buffer. It must never use the live source
buffer as the cast output.
Versions

🐛 Describe the bug
The stable PyTorch 2.13.0+cpu Linux x86_64 wheel is built with USE_XNNPACK=OFF. As a result, torch.utils.mobile_optimizer.optimize_for_mobile() fails for any traced module with an internal assertion. The same export path works with the 2.12.1 CPU wheel, which was built with XNNPACK enabled.
Minimal self-contained reproducer:
import torch
from torch.utils.mobile_optimizer import optimize_for_mobile

model = torch.jit.trace(torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 8, 3).eval(), torch.randn(1, 3, 32, 32))
optimize_for_mobile(model)
Observed result:
RuntimeError: false INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "torch/csrc/jit/passes/xnnpack_rewrite.cpp":506, please report a bug to PyTorch. Mobile optimization only available with XNNPACK at the moment. XNNPACK is not enabled. Please build with USE_XNNPACK=1

Expected result: the official Linux CPU wheel includes XNNPACK as in 2.12.1, or optimize_for_mobile() remains usable with the supported official wheel.
This was independently reproduced twice in a clean GitHub Actions environment: https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/actions/runs/29066054698
Downstream report: ultralytics/ultralytics#25088
Versions
PyTorch: 2.13.0+cpu
Torchvision: 0.28.0+cpu
Python: 3.13.14
OS: Linux 6.17.0-1018-azure x86_64, glibc 2.39
Install: official CPU wheel via uv/pip
Build setting relevant to the failure: USE_XNNPACK=OFF
Last known good: PyTorch 2.12.1+cpu (USE_XNNPACK=ON)

🐛 Describe the bug
inside a nested_compile_region that ALSO mutates its inputs (static KV cache), a custom op whose schema carries a wildcard alias annotation (Tensor! → prints as Tensor($0! -> )) is rejected:
RuntimeError: Found a custom (non-ATen) operator whose output has alias
annotations: repro_alias::scale_into(Tensor x, Tensor($0! -> ) out, float
scale) -> (). We only support functionalizing operators whose outputs do
not have alias annotations ...

Neither ingredient fails alone:

flat compile (no region) of the same model: OK
region WITHOUT the cache input-mutations: OK (op auto-functionalizes;
can_auto_functionalize(op) is True)
The failure needs region + input mutation + alias-annotated op: the
input-mutating subgraph is re-functionalized on a path that hits the C++
functionalize fallback for the custom op instead of Python auto_functionalize.

Tensor($0! -> ) is the schema shape of C++-registered kernels such as DeepGEMM's fp8_fp4_gemm_nt (kernels-community/deep-gemm).
import os


# A previously cached successful compile (e.g. from a run with a workaround
# patch active) masks the failure — the cache key ignores such state.
os.environ.setdefault("TORCHINDUCTOR_FORCE_DISABLE_CACHES", "1")

import torch
import torch.nn as nn


torch.set_grad_enabled(False)
DIM, MAX_LEN = 64, 32

lib = torch.library.Library("repro_alias", "DEF")
lib.define("scale_into(Tensor x, Tensor! out, float scale) -> ()")


def _impl(x, out, s):
    out.copy_(x * s)


lib.impl("scale_into", _impl, "CUDA")
lib.impl("scale_into", lambda x, out, s: None, "Meta")
op = torch.ops.repro_alias.scale_into
print(op.default._schema)


class Layer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(DIM, 3 * DIM)
        self.o = nn.Linear(DIM, DIM)

    def forward(self, x, k_cache, v_cache, pos):
        xs = torch.empty_like(x)
        op(x, xs, 1.0)  # alias-annotated mutating custom op (DeepGEMM-style)
        q, k, v = self.qkv(xs).chunk(3, dim=-1)
        k_cache.index_copy_(1, pos, k)  # static-cache input mutation
        v_cache.index_copy_(1, pos, v)
        attn = torch.softmax(q @ k_cache.transpose(-1, -2) / 8.0, dim=-1) @ v_cache
        return self.o(attn)


class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList(Layer() for _ in range(2))

    def forward(self, x, caches, pos):
        for layer, (k_cache, v_cache) in zip(self.layers, caches):
            x = x + layer(x, k_cache, v_cache, pos)
        return x


def inputs():
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    return (
        torch.randn(1, 4, DIM, device="cuda"),
        [
            (torch.zeros(1, MAX_LEN, DIM, device="cuda"), torch.zeros(1, MAX_LEN, DIM, device="cuda"))
            for _ in range(2)
        ],
        torch.arange(4, device="cuda"),
    )


def run(mark_region):
    torch.compiler.reset()
    if mark_region:
        Layer.forward = torch.compiler.nested_compile_region(Layer.__dict__["forward"])
    try:
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        model = Model().cuda()
        ref = model(*inputs())
        out = torch.compile(model, fullgraph=True)(*inputs())
        torch.testing.assert_close(out, ref)
        return "OK"
    except Exception as e:
        return f"FAIL {type(e).__name__}: {str(e).splitlines()[0] if str(e) else e}"
    finally:
        if mark_region:
            del Layer.forward


print(f"torch {torch.__version__}")
print(f"flat compile:   {run(mark_region=False)}")
print(f"region compile: {run(mark_region=True)}")
Versions
Single GPU. torch 2.13.0+cu130.
cc @bdhirsh @ezyang @chauhang @penguinwu @bobrenjc93 @aorenste

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Summary
This RFC proposes to make torch.accelerator the public backend-agnostic facade for default accelerator RNG management.
The API surface is:
torch.accelerator.get_rng_state(device=None)
torch.accelerator.get_rng_state_all()
torch.accelerator.set_rng_state(new_state, device=None)
torch.accelerator.set_rng_state_all(new_states)

torch.accelerator.manual_seed(seed)
torch.accelerator.manual_seed_all(seed)
torch.accelerator.seed()
torch.accelerator.seed_all()
torch.accelerator.initial_seed(device=None)
These APIs are additive. Backend-specific APIs such as torch.cuda., torch.xpu., torch.mps.*, and vendor namespaces remain supported and are not proposed for deprecation.
Motivation
PyTorch already exposes a backend-agnostic accelerator namespace for device, stream, graph, and memory operations. RNG state management is part of the same user workflow, especially for checkpointing, reproducibility, and backend-agnostic libraries.
Today, code that wants accelerator-only RNG control often has to branch:
 if device.type == "cuda":
     torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
 elif device.type == "xpu":
     torch.xpu.manual_seed_all(seed)
torch.manual_seed(seed) is still the right global convenience API for seeding CPU and supported accelerator backends together. It is not a replacement for accelerator-only state save/restore, current-device seeding, or all-accelerator-device RNG state management.
Goals

Provide a stable accelerator-level facade for default-generator RNG APIs.
Match existing backend RNG semantics where possible.
Avoid changing torch.manual_seed, CPU RNG, generator algorithms, or determinism behavior.
Support out-of-tree accelerator backends that integrate with PyTorch accelerator hooks.
Preserve existing backend namespaces without deprecation.

Non-Goals
This RFC does not propose:

changing RNG algorithms or state formats
unifying CPU and accelerator RNG state
changing torch.manual_seed() semantics
adding a new public torch.accelerator.Generator
deprecating backend-specific RNG APIs

Semantics
torch.accelerator.current_accelerator() selects the current accelerator backend and returns a torch.device with no index. RNG APIs operate on that backend.
For APIs with device=None, the current accelerator device index is used. device may be an integer index, string, or torch.device, but its device type must match the current accelerator.
Examples:
  torch.accelerator.manual_seed(1234)      # current accelerator device
  torch.accelerator.manual_seed_all(1234)  # all devices for current accelerator

  state = torch.accelerator.get_rng_state("cuda:1")
  torch.accelerator.set_rng_state(state, 1)
If no accelerator backend is available, APIs raise:
  RuntimeError: No accelerator backend is currently available.
If the requested device type does not match the current accelerator, APIs raise ValueError.
get_rng_state, get_rng_state_all, and initial_seed may eagerly initialize the accelerator runtime, matching existing backend behavior.
seed_all() should follow existing backend semantics: generate one nondeterministic seed and apply it across all accelerator devices, rather than promising distinct per-device  seeds.
Implementation Strategy
The preferred implementation is a thin Python facade over the current accelerator default generator, not Python-level branching over backend namespaces.
Conceptually:
  generator = torch._C._accelerator_getDefaultGenerator(device_index)
  generator.manual_seed(seed)
This keeps the API aligned with accelerator hooks and avoids adding CUDA/XPU/PrivateUse1-specific dispatch logic in Python.
Backend Requirements
A backend can support these APIs when it is selected by torch.accelerator.current_accelerator() and provides a default generator through the accelerator hooks interface.
For PrivateUse1 and out-of-tree backends, this means implementing the backend’s default-generator integration. Existing vendor namespace APIs may continue to exist, but torch.accelerator should depend on the common accelerator integration path rather than custom Python namespace forwarding.
Compatibility
This proposal is fully backward compatible.
Existing APIs remain valid:
  torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
  torch.xpu.manual_seed_all(seed)
  torch.mps.manual_seed(seed)
  torch.manual_seed(seed)
No migration is required. Documentation can recommend torch.accelerator for backend-agnostic code and backend namespaces for backend-specific code.
Rollout

Document the torch.accelerator RNG APIs as the backend-agnostic public facade.
Add or maintain device-generic tests covering current-device state, all-device state, seed behavior, device argument validation, and no-accelerator errors.
Opportunistically migrate internal backend-agnostic call sites where it reduces branching.
Keep backend-specific APIs documented and supported.

Open Questions

Should torch.accelerator.random.* or top-level torch.accelerator.* be the preferred documentation entry point, given both are available?

Alternatives
No response
Additional context
No response
cc @pbelevich @albanD @guangyey @EikanWang

🐛 Describe the bug
pointless_cumsum_replacement (torch/_inductor/fx_passes/post_grad.py) rewrites cumsum(full(...)) into an arange-based expression, but constructs the replacement using the full tensor's dtype and ignores the dtype= keyword passed to cumsum. When the input is created inside the compiled graph with a different dtype than the requested accumulation dtype, the compiled result has the wrong dtype vs eager:
import torch

def f():
    ones = torch.ones((2, 4, 4), dtype=torch.bool)
    return ones.cumsum(1, dtype=torch.bfloat16)

eager = f()
compiled = torch.compile(f)()
print(eager.dtype)     # torch.bfloat16
print(compiled.dtype)  # torch.int64  <- wrong
Disabling the pattern matcher (torch._inductor.config.pattern_matcher = False) makes compiled output match eager, isolating the rewrite as the cause.
Real-world impact: huggingface/transformers' DETR-family sine position embeddings used exactly this construct, making every model in that family (DETR, Sam2/Sam3, MaskFormer, …) crash under torch.compile in fp16/bf16 with mat1 and mat2 must have the same dtype, but got Float and BFloat16 — see huggingface/transformers#47228 (transformers is working around it in huggingface/transformers#47238, but the pattern is unsound for any code hitting it).
Expected: the replacement should honor cumsum's dtype kwarg (cast the arange expression accordingly), or the pattern should not match when an explicit dtype differing from the input's promotion dtype is present.
Versions
Reproduced on torch 2.13.0 (cpu and mps) and per the transformers issue on 2.x nightlies with CUDA (A100). Pattern present at torch/_inductor/fx_passes/post_grad.py:970 in 2.13.

Issue
test_honor_sm_carveout in test/test_scaled_matmul_cuda.py is missing the @onlyCUDA decorator, causing the CPU test variant to fail with:
ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 4, got 0)

Root Cause
The test profiles CUDA kernels using torch.profiler.ProfilerActivity.CUDA and unpacks exactly 4 kernel events at line 1900-1904:
no_carveout, carveout_0, carveout_66, no_carveout_again = [
    math.prod(evt.get("args", {}).get("grid", []))
    for evt in json.load(file)["traceEvents"]
    if evt.get("cat", "") == "kernel"
]
On CPU, the CUDA profiler captures zero events, causing the unpack to fail. The test is CUDA-specific by design (profiles CUDA kernel grid sizes for SM carveout behavior).
How This Happened
PR #184771 (commit 53826ac579e) correctly added @onlyCUDA:
+    @onlyCUDA
     @unittest.skipIf(IS_WINDOWS, "Windows doesn't support row-wise scaling")

🐛 Describe the bug
When make_pointwise(ops.mul) + make_reduction("sum") operates on non-contiguous (transposed) inputs after unsqueeze + broadcast expand, the generated Triton kernel uses wrong stride multipliers — it assumes contiguous strides for the logical shape instead of preserving the actual transposed strides.
The ops.dot + reduction("dot") path (native_matmul) is NOT affected because it bypasses the standard tiling heuristic and forces {y: M, x: N, r0_: K} tiling unconditionally.
Root cause
Traced through 4 independent investigations to:


Reduction unrolling (ir.py:1770-1787): When reduction_numel < unroll_reductions_threshold (default 8) AND reduction_type != "dot", the reduction is unrolled into a Pointwise node via _unroll_reduction_fn. The "dot" reduction is explicitly exempt.


View.create path difference: Without clone, the input is a ReinterpretView with is_storage_and_layout=True, so View.create uses the _compute_stride path. With clone, the input becomes a Pointwise with is_storage_and_layout=False, routing through the more robust dynamic_reshape_indexer (symbolic reindexing).


Generated code evidence: For mm(64×3, (4×3).T), the buggy kernel loads in_ptr1 + (4*k + x0) (contiguous strides (4,1) for shape (3,4)) when the actual transposed strides are (1,3). The correct load pattern is in_ptr1 + (k + 3*x0).


Related to #186850 (closed as non-reproducible, different reproducer).
Reproducer
import torch

a = torch.randn(64, 3, device='cuda')
b = torch.randn(4, 3, device='cuda')

@torch.compile
def fn(x, y):
    return torch.mm(x, y.T)

ref = torch.mm(a, b.T)
out = fn(a, b)
print(f"max diff: {(ref - out).abs().max().item()}")
# Expected: ~1e-7 (float32 tolerance)
# Actual: ~8.0 (completely wrong)
Note: This only reproduces when mm is decomposed to unsqueeze + mul + sum at the lowering level (e.g., via the small-mm pointwise optimization in PR #189149). Standard cuBLAS mm is not affected.
To reproduce without PR #189149, insert this in tuned_mm after mm_args:
mat1 = lowerings[aten.unsqueeze](mat1, -1)
mat2 = lowerings[aten.unsqueeze](mat2, 0)
args, _ = transform_args(args=[mat1, mat2], kwargs={}, broadcast=True,
                          type_promotion_kind=None, convert_input_to_bool=False)
return make_reduction("sum")(make_pointwise(ops.mul)(*args), axis=1)
Workaround
clone before unsqueeze forces the input through the dynamic_reshape_indexer path:
mat1 = L.clone(mat1)
mat2 = L.clone(mat2)
The clone has zero runtime cost because the scheduler fuses the clone's Pointwise node into the downstream mul kernel.
Versions
PyTorch 2.14.0a0+git30e161d (viable/strict), CUDA 12.8, H200

🐛 Describe the bug
A UnicodeDecodeError occurs on Windows environments (specifically with Korean locale cp949 as the system default encoding) when using torch.compile.
The root cause is that the template file torch\_inductor\kernel\templates\cutedsl_mm_grouped.py.jinja contains a non-ASCII character—specifically an em-dash (—, 0xe2), but the template loader in torch/_inductor/utils.py opens the file without explicitly specifying encoding='utf-8'. As a result, Python falls back to the system's default encoding (cp949 on Korean Windows), causing the compilation to fail.
Fix: Change the em-dash (—) to a standard hyphen (-) in cutedsl_mm_grouped.py.jinja

GitHub Issue Draft: torch.compile Segfault on XPU
Title: torch.compile causes segmentation fault on XPU with all nightly builds

🐛 Bug Description
torch.compile() causes a segmentation fault on XPU with PyTorch nightly builds, regardless of backend or PyTorch version tested.
Environment

PyTorch versions tested:

2.14.0.dev20260707+xpu ❌
2.14.0.dev20260630+xpu ❌
2.14.0.dev20260615+xpu ❌


Platform: Intel XPU (1 device available)
Python: 3.10
oneAPI: 2025.3
OS: Linux
Installation: pip install --pre torch pytorch-triton-xpu --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/xpu

Key packages:

pytorch-triton-xpu: 3.6.0+git225cdbde
triton-xpu: 3.7.2+git5fcc14d9
intel-sycl-rt: 2026.0.0

To Reproduce
Minimal reproducer:
import torch

def fn(x):
    return x * 2 + 1

x = torch.randn(4, 4, device='xpu')
print(f"Eager mode: {fn(x).shape}")  # ✅ Works

compiled_fn = torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor")
result = compiled_fn(x)  # ❌ Segmentation fault (core dumped)
Steps:

Install PyTorch XPU nightly
Run the code above
Process crashes with segmentation fault

Expected Behavior
torch.compile should successfully compile and execute the function on XPU, similar to CUDA/CPU behavior.
Actual Behavior
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
Exit code: 139


No Python exception raised
Crash occurs during first invocation (JIT compilation phase)
Affects ALL backends: inductor, eager, aot_eager

What Works
✅ Basic XPU tensor operations
✅ matmul, sigmoid, type conversions
✅ Eager mode execution (without compile)
✅ torch.xpu.is_available() returns True
What Fails
❌ torch.compile with any backend
❌ Even simplest functions (x * 2)
❌ Consistent across multiple PyTorch nightly versions
Additional Context
Related Issue: This blocks reproduction of #180948 (test_emulate_precision_casts_preserves_explicit_precision_cast_float16), which requires inductor compilation.
Investigation: Tested 3 different nightly versions spanning ~3 weeks. All exhibit the same crash, suggesting this is not a recent regression but a fundamental environmental or compatibility issue.
Hypothesis: Possible ABI incompatibility between pytorch-triton-xpu/triton-xpu and torch XPU build, or missing oneAPI configuration.
Logs/Backtraces
(To be added with gdb backtrace if requested)

Summary
At large scale, torch.compile cache reuse fails for Transformer/MoE training using distributed all_to_all collectives. Dynamo appears to encode ProcessGroup identity as a constant group name/id in the FX graph (e.g. _c10d_functional.all_to_all_single(..., '123')). When EP groups differ across ranks, this constant differs too, producing distinct graph/cache keys and causing near-total cache misses.
Scenario (realistic large-scale setup)

Total GPUs: 8192
FSDP size: 8192
EP size: 8
Number of EP groups globally: 1024 (group names like 0..1023)

In each Transformer block’s MoE path, all_to_all runs on an EP group. Because group name is baked into traced graph constants, ranks in different EP groups generate different compiled graphs.
Expected behavior
Equivalent ranks across EP groups should reuse compile cache when computation/shape semantics are identical.
Ideal pattern:
ranks 0-7: compile fresh
ranks 8-15: rank 8 should hit rank 0 cache, rank 9 hit rank 1, etc.
ranks 16-23: hit cache
...
ranks 1016-1023: hit cache

Actual behavior

Graphs differ by baked ProcessGroup name/id constant.
Cache reuse is effectively lost across EP groups.
Compiled artifact count and storage scale roughly linearly with GPU count, so compile storage overhead becomes prohibitive at large scale.

Request / possible fixes
Please consider enabling cache sharing across equivalent ProcessGroups by avoiding literal group-name specialization in graph/cache identity when safe, for example:

treat ProcessGroup/group_name as runtime input for cache keying, or
canonicalize ProcessGroup identity by role/topology rather than literal group name, or
provide an opt-in mode that ignores group-name differences for compile cache equivalence.

cc @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @kadeng @amjames @jataylo @azahed98 @oulgen @jamesjwu @aorenste @anijain2305 @laithsakka @masnesral @coconutruben @aditvenk

🐛 Describe the bug
torch.compile fails with InductorError: KeyError in Scheduler.compute_ancestors when a custom op mutates freshly-allocated (torch.empty) output buffers in place and those buffers are then reshaped in a way Inductor cannot prove is a free view (under dynamic shapes). This is the shape of a flash_attn._flash_attn_backward call writing dq/dk/dv.
Minimal standalone repro (CPU, no GPU / no flash-attn needed):
import torch

D = 512

with torch.library._scoped_library("mylib", "FRAGMENT") as lib:
    torch.library.define(
        "mylib::attn_bwd",
        "(Tensor dout, Tensor(a!) dq, Tensor(b!) dk, Tensor(c!) dv) -> Tensor",
        tags=torch.Tag.pt2_compliant_tag,
        lib=lib,
    )

    @torch.library.impl("mylib::attn_bwd", "cpu", lib=lib)
    def attn_bwd(dout, dq, dk, dv):
        src = dout.reshape(dq.shape)
        dq.copy_(src)
        dk.copy_(src)
        dv.copy_(src)
        return torch.zeros_like(dq)  # workspace, discarded by caller

    @torch.library.register_fake("mylib::attn_bwd", lib=lib)
    def _(dout, dq, dk, dv):
        return torch.empty_like(dq)

    def f(dout, weight, num_heads):
        head_dim = D // num_heads
        seqlen = dout.shape[0]
        dq = torch.empty(1, seqlen, num_heads, head_dim, dtype=dout.dtype)
        dk = torch.empty(1, seqlen, num_heads, head_dim, dtype=dout.dtype)
        dv = torch.empty(1, seqlen, num_heads, head_dim, dtype=dout.dtype)
        torch.ops.mylib.attn_bwd(dout, dq, dk, dv)  # return discarded
        a = dq.reshape(1, seqlen, D)
        b = dk.reshape(1, seqlen, D)
        c = dv.reshape(1, seqlen, D)
        return (a + b + c) @ weight

    dout = torch.randn(128, D)
    weight = torch.randn(D, D)
    torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic(dout, 0)  # dynamic seqlen forces the realize
    f(dout, weight, 8)                                   # eager: fine
    torch.compile(f, fullgraph=True, dynamic=True)(dout, weight, 8)  # raises
Traceback:
File ".../torch/_inductor/scheduler.py", line ..., in _init
    self.compute_ancestors()
File ".../torch/_inductor/scheduler.py", line ..., in compute_ancestors
    ancestors |= name_to_ancestors[dep_node_name]
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: KeyError: 'op4'

Root cause
The post-grad FX graph handed to Inductor is valid -- no node reads its own output. During lowering, the reshape [1, S, H, D//H] -> [1, S, D] cannot be proven a free view (H*(D//H) is not provably == D under dynamic S), so Inductor realizes it as a copy. That realized copy of the in-place-mutated buffer is emitted with the same buffer as both source and destination (buf = f(buf)), producing a self-referential MemoryDep.
compute_ancestors populates name_to_ancestors[op] only after iterating that op's deps, so a self-dependency raises KeyError: 'opN'. (compute_input_distances has the same lookup and fails the same way if compute_ancestors is patched.)
Notes:

It is a lowering/IR bug, not a dynamic-shapes bug per se -- dynamic shapes only force the realize. dynamic=False (static) compiles fine, and backend="aot_eager" is fine.
Not gated by config: enable_auto_functionalized_v2=False, pattern_matcher=False, inplace_buffers=False, and use_dce=False all still crash -- consistent with the fault being in core lowering rather than a toggleable pass.
Longstanding latent bug: reproduces at least back to 2.10.

The proper fix belongs in the lowering of a realized view over an in-place-mutated buffer (do not reuse the source buffer as the realized copy's destination). Making compute_ancestors/compute_input_distances tolerate self-edges is a reasonable backstop.
Versions
Reproduces on 2.14.0a0 (current main) and at least as far back as 2.10.

🐛 Describe the bug
If the process holding the lock is forcefully terminated (e.g., by OOM Killer, SIGKILL, Ctrl+C, or Slurm job cancellation), the .lock file is never cleaned up. On subsequent runs, all processes detect the stale .lock file and enter an infinite wait loop, causing a permanent deadlock.
To Reproduce

Use torch.utils.cpp_extension.load() to JIT-compile a custom C++/CUDA extension.
During compilation, forcefully kill the process (e.g., kill -9 <pid> or OOM).
Run the same script again — it will hang indefinitely at the compilation step.

Expected Behavior
No permanent deadlock: When the process holding the compilation lock is terminated (for any reason, including SIGKILL, OOM, or Slurm cancellation), subsequent runs should not hang indefinitely. The system should either:
Automatically detect and recover from the stale lock, or
Fail fast with a clear error message indicating the lock file is stale, along with instructions on how to resolve it.
Versions
python: 3.11
pytorch: 2.9.0
OS: Linux
cc @janeyx99

🐛 Describe the bug

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
symm_mem::two_shot_all_reduce_ (and the one-shot / multimem variants) synchronize the group with barriers that require the device execution order of the ops to match their group issue order. CUDA does not order kernels across streams, so issuing these ops from more than one stream — combined with realistic host-side skew between ranks — deadlocks the whole group permanently: all GPUs spin at 100%, no error is raised, launch queues fill up behind the spinning kernel.
The symmetric memory docs design synchronization channels for exactly this (barrier/put_signal/wait_signal take a channel argument with non-overlapping signal-pad slots, "so that a single handle can be used safely on multiple concurrent streams"): https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/symmetric_memory.html
However the high-level all-reduce ops neither expose a channel argument nor document a single-stream requirement:
symm_mem::two_shot_all_reduce_(Tensor(a!) input, str reduce_op, str group_name) -> Tensor(a!)
symm_mem::one_shot_all_reduce(Tensor input, str reduce_op, str group_name) -> Tensor
symm_mem::multimem_all_reduce_(Tensor(a!) input, str reduce_op, str group_name) -> Tensor(a!)

(their docstrings are empty; CUDASymmetricMemoryOps.cu on current main contains no channel plumbing).
Minimal repro (4 GPUs; unordered deadlocks in < 50 iterations, ordered — identical except for event fencing — runs 300 iterations bitwise-correct):
# torchrun --nproc-per-node 4 repro.py [unordered|ordered]
import os, sys, time
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.distributed._symmetric_memory as symm_mem

def main():
    rank = int(os.environ["RANK"])
    world = int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"])
    dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")
    torch.cuda.set_device(rank)
    device = torch.device(f"cuda:{rank}")
    mode = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "unordered"

    buf = symm_mem.empty(32 * 4096, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)
    symm_mem.rendezvous(buf, dist.group.WORLD.group_name)

    torch.manual_seed(1234)
    x = torch.randn(32 * 4096, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)
    golden = x.clone()
    dist.all_reduce(golden)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

    s1, s2 = torch.cuda.Stream(), torch.cuda.Stream()
    for i in range(300):
        # stagger ranks, mimicking host-side pauses (compilation, tuning)
        if rank == i % world and i % 7 == 0:
            time.sleep(0.02)
        st = s1 if i % 2 == 0 else s2
        if mode == "ordered":
            st.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())
        with torch.cuda.stream(st):
            buf.copy_(x)
            torch.ops.symm_mem.two_shot_all_reduce_(
                buf, "sum", dist.group.WORLD.group_name
            )
        if mode == "ordered":
            torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(st)
        if i % 50 == 0:
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
            diff = (buf.float() - golden.float()).abs().max().item()
            if rank == 0:
                print(f"iter {i}: max_diff={diff:.3e}", flush=True)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    dist.destroy_process_group()
    if rank == 0:
        print("DONE")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
How we hit it: vLLM serving (TP=4). The engine's startup phases (memory profiling, torch.compile warmup, per-range warmup) issue collectives from different streams; an Nsight Systems capture shows the same process group's collectives on three different streams with second-scale rank skew from compilation pauses, several 1–1.5 s near-miss barrier spins, and then a permanent hang (GPUs pinned at 100%, sample_tokens RPC timeout, workers alive but unresponsive). Notably NCCL survives the identical multi-stream pattern in the same trace — its LL protocol matches by per-op flag slots rather than a group phase counter, which suggests the fix direction.
Expected behavior — any of:

The all-reduce ops expose a channel argument (matching the documented channel design), or
the single-stream-per-group contract is documented on the ops and enforced with a debug assertion, or
a channel is derived internally per stream.

Workaround (validated): serialize all of a group's symm-mem ops on one dedicated stream at the caller, fenced with wait_stream events against the issuing stream — the unordered repro becomes bitwise-clean with this applied inside the caller.
Versions

torch 2.11.0+cu130 (also verified unaffected/unfixed on current main: torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemoryOps.cu has no channel plumbing)
CUDA 13, driver 595.58.03, NCCL 2.28.9
4x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120), PCIe P2P (no NVLink), Linux x86_64

cc @awgu @wanchaol @fegin @fduwjj @wz337 @wconstab @d4l3k @pragupta @msaroufim @dcci @aditvenk @weifengpy

🐛 Describe the bug
The dynamo-based ONNX exporter (torch.onnx.export(dynamo=True)) exports nn.GRU with
linear_before_reset=0, but PyTorch's GRU implementation uses linear_before_reset=1 semantics. This
causes any ONNX runtime consuming the exported model to produce numerically wrong results (up to
14% error).
The legacy TorchScript-based exporter correctly sets linear_before_reset=1.
Background
The ONNX GRU spec's linear_before_reset attribute controls where the reset gate is applied:

linear_before_reset=0: h_t = g(X@W_h + (r_t ⊙ H_{t-1})@R_h + Wb_h + Rb_h) — reset applied before
recurrent multiply
linear_before_reset=1: h_t = g(X@W_h + r_t ⊙ (H_{t-1}@R_h + Rb_h) + Wb_h) — reset applied after
recurrent multiply

PyTorch's nn.GRU uses the second form (lbr=1). See
https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.GRU.html:
▎ r_t ⊙ (W_{hr} @ h_{t-1} + b_{hr}
minimum repo:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import onnx
import onnxruntime as rt
import numpy as np
class SimpleGRU(nn.Module):
def init(self):
super().init()
self.gru = nn.GRU(input_size=4, hidden_size=8, num_layers=1, batch_first=False)
  def forward(self, x):
      output, h_n = self.gru(x)
      return output, h_n

model = SimpleGRU()
model.eval()
torch.manual_seed(42)
x = torch.randn(5, 3, 4)
PyTorch reference
with torch.no_grad():
pt_y, pt_h = model(x)
Export with dynamo (new default since PyTorch 2.9)
torch.onnx.export(model, (x,), "gru_dynamo.onnx", dynamo=True)
Verify the attribute is wrong
m = onnx.load("gru_dynamo.onnx")
for node in m.graph.node:
if node.op_type == "GRU":
for attr in node.attribute:
if attr.name == "linear_before_reset":
print(f"linear_before_reset = {attr.i}")  # Prints 0, should be 1
Run in ORT — produces wrong results
sess = rt.InferenceSession("gru_dynamo.onnx")
ort_y, ort_h = sess.run(None, {sess.get_inputs()[0].name: x.numpy()})
print(f"Max error (Y):   {np.max(np.abs(ort_y - pt_y.numpy())):.4f}")   # ~0.14
print(f"Max error (Y_h): {np.max(np.abs(ort_h - pt_h.numpy())):.4f}")   # ~0.14
Results
┌───────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
│       Exporter        │ linear_before_reset │ Max error vs PyTorch │
├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ Legacy (dynamo=False) │ 1 (correct)         │ 8.9e-08              │
├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ Dynamo (dynamo=True)  │ 0 (wrong)           │ 0.144                │
└───────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘
Expected behavior
torch.onnx.export(dynamo=True) should export nn.GRU with linear_before_reset=1, matching PyTorch's
actual GRU computation semantics.
Versions
Versions

PyTorch: 2.11.0+cpu
ONNX: 1.21.0
ONNX Runtime: 1.24.4
OS: Windows 11

cc @justinchuby @titaiwangms @mikaylagawarecki

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Redundant NaN Propagation in max op in non-onlined Softmax
Issue
Current Inductor softmax can do redundant NaN propagation in the softmax-internal max reduction.
For the fallback/persistent softmax form, the computation is effectively:
xmax = max(x, dim=-1, keepdim=True)
xexp = exp(x - xmax)
xsum = sum(xexp, dim=-1, keepdim=True)
y = xexp / xsum
The internal max is only used to stabilize softmax. It is not returned to the user as a standalone amax result.
Today, that max can lower to NaN-propagating max operations such as:
tl.maximum(a, b, tl.PropagateNan.ALL)
This is redundant for the fallback/persistent softmax path. If an input row contains a NaN, the original NaN input is still consumed by x - xmax. That NaN flows through exp, poisons xsum, and makes the final softmax row NaN. The final softmax behavior is preserved even if the internal max ignores NaNs.
So the softmax-local max can use fmax semantics:
xmax = fmax(x, dim=-1, keepdim=True)
xexp = exp(x - xmax)
xsum = sum(xexp, dim=-1, keepdim=True)
y = xexp / xsum
and lower to cheaper operations like:
tl.maximum(a, b)
triton_helpers.fmax2(...)
Performance Impact
The redundant NaN-propagating max has measurable cost. On GB200, with:
x = torch.randn(32768, N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
and online softmax enabled, start with N=1024. This shape already uses the persistent reduction path by default, so the effect of removing redundant NaN propagation is visible directly:
main/default                  27.10 us
softmax-nan/default           25.82 us   1.05x speedup

For larger N, the default lowering does not select the persistent kernel, so main and softmax-nan are mostly identical unless TORCHINDUCTOR_MULTI_KERNEL=1 is used. That knob exposes/selects the persistent multi-kernel candidate. Once both branches are on that persistent path, the speedup from removing redundant NaN propagation becomes visible.
At N=2048, the measured progression was:
main/default                  111.6 us
main + multi-kernel             75.59 us
softmax-nan + multi-kernel      64.29 us

This separates two effects:

TORCHINDUCTOR_MULTI_KERNEL=1 selects the faster persistent path: 111.6 -> 75.59 us.
Removing redundant NaN propagation from the softmax-local max further improves that persistent path: 75.59 -> 64.29 us.

Across the sweep, llu/softmax-nan + TORCHINDUCTOR_MULTI_KERNEL=1 was 1.15x geomean faster than main + TORCHINDUCTOR_MULTI_KERNEL=1.
Performance Plot

The figure plots SOL% using the bf16 softmax lower-bound traffic, 4 * M * N bytes for one input read plus one output write, divided by an assumed GB200 per-GPU HBM peak of 8.0 TB/s. The gray line is main with default TORCHINDUCTOR_MULTI_KERNEL=0, the blue line is main with TORCHINDUCTOR_MULTI_KERNEL=1, and the red line is llu/softmax-nan with TORCHINDUCTOR_MULTI_KERNEL=1.

What Must Not Change
This optimization should not be applied globally.
NaN propagation is still required for:

generic aten.amax, because its result is user-visible
generic max reductions whose result may be observed directly
online softmax max-state reductions, where the algorithm combines partial (max, sum) states and can otherwise lose the fact that a row contained a NaN

The intended scope is narrow: use non-NaN-propagating fmax only for the softmax-local fallback/persistent max reduction where the original input x still flows into the subsequent exp(x - xmax) and sum computation.
Alternatives
No response
Additional context

🐛 Describe the bug
Capturing N training iterations (forward + backward + AdamW(capturable=True).step()) of TWO independent trainers into one torch.cuda.CUDAGraph produces a graph whose replay crashes. In the script below each trainer owns M=4 plain nn.Modules called in a Python loop - no functorch anywhere - and the module is a hand-rolled LSTM-style unroll over 15 timesteps; the controls below show the LSTM cell is not essential (a gate-free RNN crashes once its unroll is deep enough). Warmup (side stream, per the torch.cuda.graph docs pattern) and capture both succeed; the crash fires at graph.replay().
The manifestation varies run to run at the same configuration: a host SIGSEGV inside cudaGraphLaunch (faulthandler shows torch/cuda/graphs.py:139 in replay, sometimes on the first replay, sometimes after "replay 1" completes), or an asynchronous cudaErrorIllegalAddress surfacing as torch.AcceleratorError at the torch.cuda.synchronize() after a replay. The wandering crash point and mixed host/device manifestation look like memory corruption in the captured graph.
Controls, each verified by flipping one ingredient at a time (all on this GPU and stack), clean unless said otherwise:

ITERS = 1 (one iteration per graph): clean at every scale tested; the application this was distilled from runs that variant stably over ~48k replays.
TRAINERS = 1: clean in every configuration tested, including 15x32 scale.
Smaller scale: ITERS, SWEEPS of 2, 32 / 15, 1 / 8, 8 are all clean; 15, 32 crashes every run (10 of 10 across script variants). The threshold sits somewhere between 64 and 480 captured iteration pairs.
Replacing the unrolled module with a 2-layer MLP: clean in every configuration tested, including ITERS = 240 (~16x the crashing iteration count, i.e. comparable total captured work), so total captured node volume is not the discriminator.
Unroll depth is the discriminator: a plain tanh RNN cell (no gates) with a 15-step unroll is clean, the same RNN at a 60-step unroll crashes. So it is not LSTM-specific; the depth of the sequential chain in each backward is what matters.
Also crashes with functorch-stacked ensembles (M copies per trainer via stack_module_state + functional_call under torch.vmap, M=4 or M=10), so the bug is not functorch-related. Several of the controls above were verified on that variant of the same setup.
Plain SGD instead of AdamW(capturable=True): still crashes, so captured optimizer state is not required.
Static input batches vs freshly gather-indexed ones: crashes either way (the script below uses static).

Capture legality: static shapes throughout, no D2H reads or syncs, no host branching on device values, no RNG ops inside the capture region. Stock pip wheel, no extensions. If this multi-iteration, multi-optimizer capture pattern is unsupported, I would expect an error at capture time; instead capture succeeds and the replay segfaults or corrupts memory.
Repro (crashes in seconds on an A10):
# SIGSEGV / illegal memory access at replay of a CUDA graph capturing ITERS
# training iterations of TRAINERS independent training loops over unrolled
# recurrent modules. Plain nn.Modules, no functorch.
# Clean in our testing (verified on this setup and/or a functorch-stacked variant
# of it): ITERS = 1; TRAINERS = 1; (ITERS, SWEEPS) = (2, 32) / (15, 1) / (8, 8)
import faulthandler

import torch

faulthandler.enable()

TRAINERS, ITERS, SWEEPS, REPLAYS, WARMUPS = 2, 15, 32, 3, 3
M, B, FEAT, HID, ACT, L = 4, 32, 16, 32, 5, 15


class Lstm(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.ih = torch.nn.Linear(FEAT, 4 * HID)
        self.hh = torch.nn.Linear(HID, 4 * HID)
        self.head = torch.nn.Linear(HID, ACT)

    def forward(self, x):
        h = torch.zeros(x.shape[0], HID, device=x.device)
        c = torch.zeros(x.shape[0], HID, device=x.device)
        outs = []
        for t in range(L):
            gates = self.ih(x[:, t]) + self.hh(h)
            i, f, g, o = gates.chunk(4, dim=-1)
            c = torch.sigmoid(f) * c + torch.sigmoid(i) * torch.tanh(g)
            h = torch.sigmoid(o) * torch.tanh(c)
            outs.append(self.head(h))
        return torch.stack(outs, dim=1)


def trainer(dev):
    nets = [Lstm().to(dev) for _ in range(M)]
    params = [p for n in nets for p in n.parameters()]
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr=1e-3, capturable=True)
    batch = torch.randn(M, B, L, FEAT, device=dev)

    def sweep():
        loss = torch.stack([n(batch[i]) for i, n in enumerate(nets)]).pow(2).mean()
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=False)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()

    return sweep


def main():
    dev = torch.device("cuda")
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    trainers = [trainer(dev) for _ in range(TRAINERS)]

    def iteration():
        for _ in range(SWEEPS):
            for sweep in trainers:
                sweep()

    side = torch.cuda.Stream()
    side.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())
    with torch.cuda.stream(side):
        for _ in range(WARMUPS):
            iteration()
    torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(side)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print("warmup done", flush=True)
    graph = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
    with torch.cuda.graph(graph):
        for _ in range(ITERS):
            iteration()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print("capture done", flush=True)
    for i in range(1, REPLAYS + 1):
        graph.replay()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        print(f"replay {i} done", flush=True)
    print("CLEAN - did not reproduce", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

🐛 Describe the bug
Per the docs, when A has shape (*, n, n) and B has shape (n,) or (n, k), B is broadcast to A's batch shape. On MPS this returns silently wrong results: only the first batch element is solved and the remaining batch elements come back all-zero. With equal batch shapes the result matches CPU.
The reproduction below uses the shapes from the documentation's own broadcasting example (b is broadcasted to size (2, 3, 1)), plus a pure vector RHS (B.ndim == 1, internally unsqueezed to (n, 1)), which fails the same way:
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)

A = torch.randn(2, 3, 3)
b = torch.randn(3, 1)

x = torch.linalg.solve(A, b)
print("cpu allclose(A @ x, b):", torch.allclose(A @ x, b, atol=1e-5))

A_mps, b_mps = A.to("mps"), b.to("mps")
x_mps = torch.linalg.solve(A_mps, b_mps)
print("mps allclose(A @ x, b):", torch.allclose((A_mps @ x_mps).cpu(), b, atol=1e-5))
print("x cpu:", x.flatten().tolist())
print("x mps:", x_mps.cpu().flatten().tolist())

# vector RHS (B.ndim == 1) hits the same path (internally unsqueezed to (n, 1))
v = torch.randn(3)
x_cpu = torch.linalg.solve(A, v)
x_mps = torch.linalg.solve(A_mps, v.to("mps")).cpu()
print("vector-rhs x cpu:", x_cpu.flatten().tolist())
print("vector-rhs x mps:", x_mps.flatten().tolist())

# control: equal batch shapes -> matches CPU
B = torch.randn(2, 3, 1)
x_cpu = torch.linalg.solve(A, B)
x_mps = torch.linalg.solve(A_mps, B.to("mps")).cpu()
print("equal-batch max |cpu - mps|:", (x_cpu - x_mps).abs().max().item())
Output:
cpu allclose(A @ x, b): True
mps allclose(A @ x, b): False
x cpu: [-1.3485809564590454, 0.21591687202453613, -1.5190253257751465, 1.2567596435546875, -1.3927536010742188, 1.9916460514068604]
x mps: [-1.3485809564590454, 0.21591687202453613, -1.5190253257751465, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
vector-rhs x cpu: [1.1054476499557495, -0.18842813372612, 0.6292412281036377, -0.847964882850647, 2.061440944671631, -2.437061309814453]

equal-batch max |cpu - mps|: 8.940696716308594e-08

🐛 Describe the bug
Follow-up to #181789 (related: #172819 / #173391): one more case where
_dynamic_scale_rblock mutates the autotune candidate set after the cache contract is
frozen, defeating autotune_local_cache=True. Verified on current nightly.
check_autotune_cache only creates an AutotuneCache when there is more than one config
(torch/_inductor/runtime/triton_heuristics.py):
if (
    not disabled
    and filename is not None
    and (len(configs) > 1 or inductor_meta.get("coordinate_descent_tuning"))
    and os.environ.get("TRITON_INTERPRET", "0") != "1"
):
    configs_hash = hash_configs(configs)
    autotune_cache = AutotuneCache.create(inductor_meta, filename, configs_hash)
Reduction kernels with ReductionHint.INNER (also OUTER / OUTER_TINY) get exactly
one heuristic config from _reduction_configs, so autotune_cache is None and the
autotuner's save_cache_hook is None. If the compiled kernel is register-pressure
limited, _dynamic_scale_rblock later appends a halved-R0_BLOCK candidate during
precompile() → 2 launchers → the first hot call runs autotune_to_one_config():

with no cache to read — so the #181789 "skip _dynamic_scale_rblock when
autotune_cache_state == "hit"" fix can never engage, because a hit is impossible; and
with no save hook — so a .best_config is never written.

Every process therefore re-benchmarks {R0_BLOCK, R0_BLOCK/2} forever. That is wasted
warm-start time, and worse: when the two candidates are near-tied, the winner flips from
process to process — nondeterministic performance and numerics (R0_BLOCK changes the
reduction split), with the local autotune cache enabled the whole time.
Minimal repro
1×H200 (SM90), 2.14.0.dev20260706+cu130, triton 3.8.0+git43422b04. Driver runs 3
fresh processes against one persistent TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR; instrumentation is
print-only wrappers around stock functions.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Repro: single-heuristic-config reduction + _dynamic_scale_rblock =>
# no AutotuneCache, re-benchmark {R0_BLOCK, R0_BLOCK/2} in EVERY process,
# no .best_config ever written, despite autotune_local_cache=True.
# Run: python repro.py   (driver: 3 fresh processes over one warm cache dir)
import glob
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys

CACHE = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "repro_cache")
os.environ.setdefault("TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR", CACHE)
os.environ.setdefault("TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS", "1")  # readable logs only


def instrument():
    # observability only -- wrappers print what stock torch does
    from torch._inductor.runtime import triton_heuristics as th

    real_check = th.check_autotune_cache

    def check(configs, filename, inductor_meta):
        out = real_check(configs, filename, inductor_meta)
        print(
            f"[AT] check n_configs={len(configs)} "
            f"state={out[2].get('autotune_cache_state')}",
            flush=True,
        )
        return out

    th.check_autotune_cache = check

    real_dsr = th.CachingAutotuner._dynamic_scale_rblock

    def dsr(self):
        before = len(self.compile_results)
        out = real_dsr(self)
        if len(self.compile_results) != before:
            print(f"[AT] DSR-INJECT {before}->{len(self.compile_results)}", flush=True)
        return out

    th.CachingAutotuner._dynamic_scale_rblock = dsr

    real_bench = th.CachingAutotuner.benchmark_all_configs

    def bench(self, *a, **kw):
        out = real_bench(self, *a, **kw)
        timings = sorted((t, l.config.kwargs.get("R0_BLOCK")) for l, t in out.items())
        print(
            f"[AT] AUTOTUNE save_hook={self.save_cache_hook is not None} "
            + ", ".join(f"R0={r}:{t:.4f}ms" for t, r in timings),
            flush=True,
        )
        return out

    th.CachingAutotuner.benchmark_all_configs = bench


def kernel(a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h):
    # Single-heuristic-config reduction (ReductionHint.INNER, register_intensive)
    # that triggers _dynamic_scale_rblock injection at precompile.
    s = a + b + c + d + e + f + g + h
    sf = s.float()
    v = (sf * sf).mean(-1, keepdim=True)
    y = (sf * torch.rsqrt(v + 1e-6)).to(torch.bfloat16)
    return y, sf.sum(-1), sf.abs().amax(-1)


def phase():
    import torch

    globals()["torch"] = torch
    instrument()
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    args = tuple(
        torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) for _ in range(8)
    )
    torch.compile(kernel, fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)(*args)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    n = len(glob.glob(os.path.join(CACHE, "**", "*.best_config"), recursive=True))
    print(f"[AT] best_config files on disk: {n}", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:
        phase()
    else:
        shutil.rmtree(CACHE, ignore_errors=True)
        for i in range(3):
            p = subprocess.run(
                [sys.executable, __file__, "phase"], capture_output=True, text=True
            )
            print(f"===== process {i} (rc={p.returncode}) =====")
            print(
                "\n".join(
                    ln
                    for ln in (p.stdout + p.stderr).splitlines()
                    if ln.startswith("[AT]")
                )
            )
            if p.returncode != 0:
                print((p.stdout + p.stderr)[-3000:])
Output (verbatim):
===== process 0 (rc=0) =====
[AT] check n_configs=1 state=only 1 config
[AT] DSR-INJECT 1->2
[AT] AUTOTUNE save_hook=False R0=1024:0.0947ms, R0=512:0.0990ms
[AT] best_config files on disk: 0
===== process 1 (rc=0) =====
[AT] check n_configs=1 state=only 1 config
[AT] check n_configs=1 state=only 1 config
[AT] DSR-INJECT 1->2
[AT] AUTOTUNE save_hook=False R0=1024:0.0945ms, R0=512:0.0991ms
[AT] best_config files on disk: 0
===== process 2 (rc=0) =====
[AT] check n_configs=1 state=only 1 config
[AT] check n_configs=1 state=only 1 config
[AT] DSR-INJECT 1->2
[AT] AUTOTUNE save_hook=False R0=1024:0.0944ms, R0=512:0.0992ms
[AT] best_config files on disk: 0

Processes 1 and 2 are warm starts (FXGraphCache hit; the static-autotuner
recheck_autotune_cache also runs and reports only 1 config): they still re-inject and
re-benchmark, and no .best_config can ever exist. A multi-config kernel compiled in the
same processes caches normally (hit on process 1+2, no re-benchmark) — the difference is
purely the len(configs) > 1 gate.
Real-world impact (measured)
Production LLM serving (vLLM 0.24.0, torch 2.11.0+cu130, gemma-4-31B NVFP4 on 1×H200):
the fused add+GEMM-epilogue+RMSNorm reduction
(triton_red_fused_add_marlin_gemm_mul_rms_norm_2, r0_numel=5376, register-intensive,
one heuristic config R0_BLOCK=1024, injected 512) re-tunes on every server boot.
In the synthetic repro above the winner happens to be stable; on this production kernel
the two candidates are near-tied and boots land on either side — median single-stream
decode throughput flips ~3.4% (242.6 vs 250.9 tok/s) and greedy numerics shift
(speculative-decode acceptance 3.897 vs 3.985 accepted tokens/step) across identical
deployments with warm caches. We currently work around it by pinning the config through a
patched-in env override to get deterministic serving.
Suggested fix
Make the cache contract cover any kernel that can reach autotune_to_one_config:

create the AutotuneCache when the kernel is _dynamic_scale_rblock-eligible
(_could_rblock_scale) even if len(configs) == 1, or
when _dynamic_scale_rblock actually extends a single-config kernel, create the cache
at that point (hashing the extended candidate list) so the winner is persisted and
re-read on the next process.

Related (appears already fixed on nightly, noting for 2.11/2.12 users)
On 2.11.0 we also hit the sibling case: statically-launchable autotuners whose serialized
compile_results include the injected config recompute hash_configs over N+1 configs
in recheck_autotune_cache, never match the N-config hash stored in .best_config, and
re-benchmark + rewrite (with the old hash) on every warm boot — 15 of 38 multi-config
kernels on the model above. On 2.14.0.dev20260706 we could not reproduce this: the
injected config no longer reaches the bundle (recheck sees the original list, hash
matches, hit), so it looks fixed by the #181789-era changes.
Versions

repro: torch 2.14.0.dev20260706+cu130 nightly, triton 3.8.0+git43422b04, CUDA 13.0,
1×H200 (SM90), Ubuntu 24.04, Python 3.12
production measurements: torch 2.11.0+cu130, triton 3.6.0, same machine

nodes.title: [inductor] Single-config reductions extended by _dynamic_scale_rblock are permanently uncacheable — re-benchmark {R0_BLOCK, R0_BLOCK/2} every process; near-tied winners flip perf and numerics

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
On the release/2.13 ROCm wheels, import torch hangs forever on any host that lacks the AMD kfd driver — CPU-only nodes, or GPU nodes
where amdgpu/amdkfd isn't loaded. The 2.12.1+rocm7.2 ROCm wheel imports cleanly on the same host, so this is a 2.13 regression.
Nightly torch-2.14.0.dev20260706%2Brocm7.2-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl also is currently failing same way.
 import torch
 W... agent.cpp:608] sysfs nodes path '/sys/class/kfd/kfd/topology/nodes' does not exist

hangs indefinitely, never returns
Where it hangs
The hang is in a static initializer that runs at dlopen time, before any Python/env-configurable torch code executes. Native backtrace
(py-spy dump --native):
Thread (idle): "MainThread"
__gthread_join (gthr-default.h:715)
std::thread::join (thread.cc:134)
librocprofiler-sdk.so   (x5 frames)
libtorch_rocshmem.so
ld-linux  (_dl_catch_exception / call_init)   # C++ static initializers
dlopen (libc.so.6)
_call_with_frames_removed (importlib._bootstrap:488)
create_module (importlib._bootstrap_external:1293)
 (torch/init.py:445)              # from torch._C import *
Sequence: import torch → dlopen(libtorch_hip.so) → libtorch_rocshmem.so static constructor calls into the ROCm runtime →
librocprofiler-sdk.so spawns a worker thread (the one printing agent.cpp:608 while probing /sys/class/kfd/kfd/topology/nodes) and
std::thread::join()s it. With no kfd device the worker never completes, so the join blocks forever.
libtorch_rocshmem.so is an unconditional hard dependency, so this path runs on every import torch:
$ readelf -d libtorch_hip.so | grep -i rocshmem
0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)  Shared library: [libtorch_rocshmem.so]
(matches target_link_libraries(torch_hip PRIVATE torch_rocshmem) in caffe2/CMakeLists.txt). There is no runtime/env workaround — deleting the
lib just breaks the load differently.
Regression analysis (2.12 vs 2.13)
Both wheels ship torch/lib/libtorch_rocshmem.so, and its direct NEEDED list is byte-identical between 2.12 and 2.13 — and notably neither
links librocprofiler-sdk.so directly. rocprofiler-sdk is auto-loaded transitively via HSA / librocprofiler-register.so. Comparing the bundled
profiler libs:



lib
2.12.1+rocm7.2
release/2.13




librocprofiler-register.so
944,840
944,840 — identical


librocprofiler-sdk.so
8,378,529
8,133,513 — changed



So the register shim is unchanged; only librocprofiler-sdk.so (and the surrounding ROCm runtime version) changed. Swapping the 2.12
librocprofiler-sdk.so into the 2.13 install changes the symptom from hang to a libdrm.so-missing load error, confirming that (a) 2.13
actively loads librocprofiler-sdk.so at import, and (b) the two sdk builds differ in behavior/transitive deps. (A fully clean before/after swap
was blocked by the unrelated missing libdrm.so on the test host.)
rocprofiler-sdk versions:

2.12: <fill in: strings librocprofiler-sdk.so | grep -i version>
2.13: <fill in>

Impact
Any environment that does import torch without an AMD GPU present hard-hangs: CPU-only CI smoke tests, docs builds, packaging/release
validation, and mixed CPU/GPU fleets. This blocks release validation of the 2.13 ROCm wheels.
Suggested fix

Do not initialize rocSHMEM / rocprofiler-sdk from a static constructor at library load. Make init lazy (on first symmetric-memory use) or
gate it on device availability (skip when /dev/kfd / no HIP devices).
librocprofiler-sdk init (the topology thread) must not block indefinitely when kfd is absent — likely an AMD-side fix.
Short term: consider pinning/reverting librocprofiler-sdk.so to the 2.12 build, or preventing HSA from auto-loading the profiler tool during a
plain import torch.

Versions

Broken: PyTorch release/2.13 ROCm wheel (<fill in exact: e.g. 2.13.0+rocm7.x>), Python 3.12.
Working: PyTorch 2.12.1+rocm7.2, same host.
Host: no AMD GPU / kfd driver — no /sys/class/kfd, no /dev/kfd, amdgpu/amdkfd not loaded.
